fuentes.texto: NASA — Pioneer 11, the first to explore Saturn

turnos.pregunta: I was the first spacecraft in history to reach Saturn. What did I find there?
opciones: A new ring and a moon
turnos.texto_explorador: A new ring, the F ring, and a small moon that nobody had seen. I also noticed the first clear sign that Saturn has a magnetic field of its own.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I detected Saturn's bow shock on August 31, 1979, at 1.5 million km, the first conclusive evidence of its magnetic field; I discovered the F ring and a moon about 200 km across, and took 440 images of the system.

turnos.pregunta: Before Saturn you went past Jupiter. What did you see from so close?
opciones: Its poles, for the first time
turnos.texto_explorador: Its poles. I passed 42.500 kilometres from the clouds, three times closer than my sister Pioneer 10, and from there you can see the regions at the top and at the bottom of the planet.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On the flyby of December 3, 1974 I passed 42.500 km from the clouds at more than 171.000 km/h: the first images of Jupiter's polar regions and about 200 images of its moons.

turnos.pregunta: You carry a plaque with drawings. What do they explain?
opciones: Where we come from and when
turnos.texto_explorador: Where we come from. It has two human figures, the position of the Sun and some marks that place our star relative to fourteen pulsars: a map for whoever finds it.
turnos.texto_cientifico: The Pioneer plaque, designed by Carl Sagan, Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan, shows a human couple, the silhouette of the spacecraft, the position of the Sun and where it sits relative to 14 pulsars.

hitos.texto: To follow Pioneer 10's path to Jupiter and, if the passage through the asteroid belt went well, to use its push to reach Saturn.
hitos.fuente: NASA History — 45 Years Ago: Pioneer 11 Launched

hitos.texto: In March 1974 I went through the asteroid belt without damage. Without that news, no later mission would have dared to cross.
hitos.fuente: NASA History — 45 Years Ago: Pioneer 11 Launched

hitos.texto: On September 30, 1995 the mission was closed and on November 24 a few minutes of engineering data came in: my last voice, from more than 6.400 million kilometres away.

puntos3d.texto: The 2.74-metre dish, the most visible part of the spacecraft. With it came the 440 images of the Saturn system.
The radioisotope thermoelectric generators on a boom. They ran for 22 years against the 21 months planned.
The instrument package, with the particle detectors and the magnetometer that found Saturn's magnetic field.

aparatos.lugar: In a heliocentric orbit over the Sun's poles, silent since 2009

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I stopped answering on June 30, 2009, after more than eighteen years of work. I am still circling the Sun, passing over its poles.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: The mission ended on June 30, 2009: the switch to the low-gain antenna was commanded at 20:09 UTC and the transmitter was switched off at 20:15 UTC. Its heliocentric orbit is carrying it away from Earth.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first spacecraft to look at the Sun's poles, above and below the plane of the planets, and there the solar wind blew at twice the speed. It was meant to last five years and lasted more than eighteen.

personas.papel: mission manager and Ulysses project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA)
Ulysses project scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

turnos.pregunta: To look at the Sun's poles I had to leave the plane where the planets turn. How did I manage it?
turnos.texto_explorador: With a push from Jupiter. I passed 378.400 kilometres from the planet and its gravity flung me above the plane of the others, like a stone let go from a sling.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On February 8, 1992 I flew past Jupiter at about 378.400 km. Its gravitational assist took me into an inclined heliocentric orbit, outside the ecliptic: I was the fifth spacecraft to reach Jupiter and the first to look at the Sun from above and from below.

turnos.pregunta: From up there the Sun's wind does not blow the same as at the equator. How much faster did I find it at the poles?
turnos.texto_explorador: About twice as fast. Up there it blew at about 750 kilometres per second and at the equator at about 350: the difference between a gale and a soft breeze.
turnos.texto_cientifico: With the first three-dimensional map of the heliosphere I measured about 750 km/s in the polar regions against about 350 km/s for the equatorial wind. The polar magnetic field turned out to be much weaker than assumed, and it flips every eleven years.

turnos.pregunta: Do you know what my farewell was? I was not expecting to run into anything like that on my way.
opciones: Crossing the tail of three comets
turnos.texto_explorador: Crossing the tail of three comets without looking for it. I found that those tails are much longer than people thought, like a trail of smoke that reaches much further than expected.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I crossed, unexpectedly, the tails of comets Hyakutake (May 1996), McNaught-Hartley (1999) and McNaught (2007), and showed that cometary tails are much longer than expected. I also recorded more than 1.800 gamma-ray bursts.

hitos.texto: To study the Sun above and below the plane of the planets, something no spacecraft had done. It was launched in the cargo bay of the shuttle Discovery on October 6, 1990.
Between 1994 and 1995 I passed over the south pole and the north pole of the Sun and reached 80.2 degrees of solar latitude. On March 12, 1995 I came within about 200 million kilometres of the Sun.
On June 30, 2009 my transmitter was switched off, after more than eighteen and a half years of service: more than four times the planned lifetime. My orbit keeps carrying me away from Earth.

puntos3d.texto: The dish that always pointed at Earth while the spacecraft looped over the Sun's poles.
The radioisotope generator on a separate boom so it would not heat the instruments. It powered 18 and a half years of mission.
The long spinning body, with the experiments that measured the solar wind and the dust arriving from outside the Solar System.

aparatos.lugar: Resting on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, in the Ma'at region

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I came down slowly until I touched my comet on September 30, 2016. I stopped answering when I reached the ground and there I stay, in a place called Ma'at.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Controlled descent and touchdown on September 30, 2016 in the Ma'at region, next to the Deir el-Medina pit; the day before it was about 23 km from the nucleus. The mission ended with that planned impact.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first spacecraft to orbit a comet and the first to set a robot down on its surface. In the ice of 67P it found glycine, one of the building blocks of life.

personas.papel: principal investigator of the ROSINA instrument at the University of Bern, for the European Space Agency
principal investigator of the MIRO instrument at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

ESA — Rosetta's comet water reopens the debate on the origin of the oceans

turnos.pregunta: I reached a comet and I did not carry on past it like the others. What did I do that nobody had done before?
turnos.texto_explorador: Start circling around it. I was the first spacecraft to orbit a comet and to travel with it along its path, like a small moon turning around a mountain of ice and dust.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On August 6, 2014 I became the first spacecraft to orbit a comet and to escort it along its journey: I accompanied 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko to its perihelion on August 13, 2015, and on its way back as well.

turnos.pregunta: I analysed the water of my comet and something odd came out. What was special about it?
opciones: It was different from ocean water
It was salty like the sea
turnos.texto_explorador: That it was different from ocean water. Its hydrogen was heavier than that of Earth's seas, so this comet does not seem to have brought the water we drink.
turnos.texto_cientifico: With the ROSINA instrument I measured a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio more than three times higher than that of Earth's oceans: 67P does not fit as the main source of Earth's water and the debate about its origin is still open.

turnos.pregunta: Before saying goodbye I found a molecule that is very important for life. Which one was it?
turnos.texto_explorador: Glycine, the simplest amino acid: one of the pieces that proteins are built from. It was the first time one had been found in the gas cloud of a comet.
turnos.texto_cientifico: In 2016 I detected glycine unambiguously in the comet's coma, the first time an amino acid had been found in one of these bodies. On the surface, Philae's COSAC instrument identified 16 organic compounds, four of them never seen in comets before.

hitos.texto: To reach comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, go into orbit around it and set the Philae lander down on its surface. I travelled 7.900 million kilometres and gathered 220 GB of data.
On November 12, 2014 Philae separated from me and touched down on the comet: it took the first images from the surface of one of these bodies and completed close to 80% of its first science sequence.
In the Ma'at region I found active pits more than 100 metres across and between 50 and 60 metres deep, with one-metre mounds that could be the pieces the comet was built from.

puntos3d.texto: The steerable 2.2-metre dish that sent 220 gigabytes of comet data.
The two 14-metre wings. Eight hundred million kilometres from the Sun they produced only 395 watts, so the spacecraft slept for two and a half years.
The robot that dropped onto the comet on 12 November 2014 and bounced twice before settling in a spot with no sunlight.

aparatos.lugar: Its spacecraft ran out of fuel in solar orbit; the capsule with the samples is in Houston

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I finished on March 24, 2011 with one last burn. I was left without fuel and in silence, circling the Sun, but my cargo got home.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Last transmission on March 24, 2011, after a final 146-second burn that used up the propellant, received 312 million km from Earth. The spacecraft was left uncontrolled in a heliocentric orbit; the capsule had been in Houston since 2006.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It brought comet dust to Earth for the first time: more than ten thousand particles trapped in a foam almost as light as air. Among them was glycine.

turnos.pregunta: I passed very close to a comet to catch its dust. What did I collect it in?
turnos.texto_explorador: In a foam almost as light as air: aerogel. The grains sank into it and came to a stop without breaking, like a fly landing in honey.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On January 2, 2004 I passed about 250 km from the nucleus of comet Wild 2 and captured its grains in a silica aerogel, where they stayed embedded without melting. A capsule brought them to Earth and made it possible to analyse them in the laboratory.

turnos.pregunta: And what turned up inside that dust when they opened it on Earth?
turnos.texto_explorador: Glycine, the simplest amino acid. In the dust of my comet there was one of the basic pieces for building proteins, and it was the first time one had been found in a comet.
turnos.texto_cientifico: In the Wild 2 samples glycine was identified, the first amino acid found in a comet, together with a wide variety of organic compounds. In August 2014 seven interstellar dust particles were announced among the material collected.

turnos.pregunta: At the end of my life I went back to visit a comet. What for?
opciones: To photograph a crater from another mission
turnos.texto_explorador: To see the crater that another mission had dug years earlier. It was the first time a spacecraft returned to a comet, and I photographed it from 181 kilometres away.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On February 15, 2011 I flew past comet Tempel 1 at 181 km: it was the first visit to an already explored comet. I photographed the crater left by the Deep Impact impactor and mapped areas that had not been seen before.

hitos.texto: To go to comet Wild 2, collect dust from its wake and bring it back to Earth in a capsule. It was launched on February 7, 1999 from Cape Canaveral.
On January 2, 2004 I passed about 250 kilometres from the nucleus and caught more than 10.000 particles larger than a micrometre. On January 15, 2006 the capsule landed in Utah at 10:10 UTC.

hitos.texto: On February 15, 2011 I passed 181 kilometres from comet Tempel 1, the first time one of these bodies has been revisited. On March 24, a final 146-second burn closed the mission.

aparatos.lugar: In solar orbit, with its engine off since December 2001

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I switched off my engine on December 18, 2001 and finished my work. I left the radio receiver on in case someone, some day, wants to call me.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Final shutdown of the ion engine on December 18, 2001, after 16.265 hours of operation and about 4.3 km/s of velocity change. An attempt to make contact in March 2002 was unsuccessful.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It flew with an engine that pushed with xenon ions, almost without force but without stopping, and it tested twelve new technologies at once. It also steered itself, with no help from Earth.

director of NASA's Solar System Exploration Division, in Washington
director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

turnos.pregunta: My engine did not make flames: it pushed with a jet of xenon ions, very gentle but steady. What did I achieve that way?
opciones: A tiny push for a very long time
An enormous speed in one second
turnos.texto_explorador: A tiny push for a very long time. It is like pushing a cart without stopping for days: each push feels smaller, but in the end it picks up a speed that does not run out.
turnos.texto_cientifico: My ion engine reached a specific impulse of 3.100 seconds, up to ten times that of chemical propellants. It ran for fourteen days in a row in November 1998 and accumulated 16.265 hours of operation.

turnos.pregunta: One day I lost one of my star trackers. What did the team do with me?
opciones: Rebuild the way I orient myself without it
turnos.texto_explorador: Rebuild the way I orient myself without that sensor. They programmed me to steer with other data and I kept flying: they saved my mission from Earth, with a watchmaker's patience.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On November 11, 1999 my star tracker failed. The team rebuilt the attitude control system without it, relying on the AutoNav autonomous navigation software, which later became the basis for the Deep Impact mission.

turnos.pregunta: At the end of my life I passed by a comet. What do you think I brought back from there?
turnos.texto_explorador: Its photos. I passed 2.171 kilometres from the nucleus of comet Borrelly and brought back images of its dark heart, some of the best that had been taken until then.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On September 22, 2001 I flew past comet Borrelly at 2.171 km from the nucleus and a relative speed of 16.58 km/s: I returned some of the best images of a comet obtained until then, along with data taken close to the nucleus.

hitos.texto: To test twelve high-risk technologies in flight all at once, among them an ion engine and a program that steered the spacecraft with no help from Earth. All twelve tests turned out well.
My xenon engine totalled 16.265 hours and a velocity change of about 4.3 km/s, the largest ever achieved by a spacecraft with its own propulsion. I used 90% of the xenon I carried.

It was designed for an eleven-month mission and it operated for more than three years. On December 18, 2001 the engine was switched off and, after the failed attempt of March 2002, there was no further contact.

aparatos.lugar: In a solar orbit trailing behind Earth, in safe mode since January 2020

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I went into safe mode on January 30, 2020 and I no longer do science. I circle the Sun a little behind Earth, with my eyes closed.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: On January 30, 2020 it went into safe mode and the mission ended, after more than 16 years against the two and a half years planned. Its data remain in the IRSA/IPAC archive at Caltech.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first telescope to detect light from a planet around another star and the one that announced seven Earth-sized worlds around a single sun. It was supposed to last two and a half years and worked for more than sixteen.

personas.papel: Spitzer project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
Spitzer project scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

director of Astrophysics at NASA

JPL — fifteen great discoveries from Spitzer

turnos.pregunta: My eyes only see heat, not light like yours. What is the use of looking at the sky that way?
opciones: To see what is cold and what hides behind dust
To see the brightest stars better
turnos.texto_explorador: To see what is cold and what hides behind the dust. Dust blocks ordinary light but lets heat through, so I can look inside the clouds where stars are born.
turnos.texto_cientifico: My 85 cm telescope observed in the infrared, where dust is transparent and cold bodies emit. I worked at 5 K, cooled by 360 litres of liquid helium that ran out on May 15, 2009 and gave way to the warm phase.

turnos.pregunta: Around a small red star I found something very special. What was it?
opciones: Seven planets the size of Earth
turnos.texto_explorador: Seven rocky planets the size of Earth, all around the same star. Three of them are in the band where water could be liquid, neither very hot nor very cold.
turnos.texto_cientifico: In February 2017 I announced the first known system of seven Earth-sized planets around a single star, TRAPPIST-1; three of them are in the habitable zone, where liquid water is possible on the surface.

turnos.pregunta: Before I fell asleep I discovered a new ring at Saturn. What was it like?
opciones: Gigantic and made of thin dust
turnos.texto_explorador: Gigantic and made of thin dust, so loose that it is barely noticeable. It spans about 300 times the width of Saturn, so it is more a very fine cloud than a ring of the usual kind.
turnos.texto_cientifico: In 2009 I discovered a faint ring of Saturn, the Phoebe ring, about 300 times the diameter of the planet: a structure of scattered dust, very different from the bright rings you see with an ordinary telescope.

hitos.texto: To observe the universe in the infrared as the fourth of NASA's Great Observatories. It was launched on August 25, 2003 and on December 18 it received the name Spitzer.
On May 15, 2009 the liquid helium that cooled my instruments to 5 K ran out. I kept working with two modules of the main instrument in what is called the warm phase.
hitos.fuente: JPL — fifteen great discoveries from Spitzer

hitos.texto: On January 30, 2020 I entered safe mode and closed the mission, with more than 16 years of service. My data are still available in the IRSA/IPAC archive.

aparatos.lugar: In a parking orbit around the Sun since September 2010

estado_texto.texto_explorador: It took the oldest photo of the universe and retired in 2010. Now it circles the Sun, switched off, talking to nobody.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: It closed its data taking on August 20, 2010, after nine years measuring the cosmic microwave background from L2; on September 8, 2010 it moved to a heliocentric parking orbit.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It put a date on the universe: 13.770 million years, with only 4.6% ordinary atoms. It observed from the L2 point for nine years and was switched off in 2010.

personas.papel: principal investigator of WMAP at Johns Hopkins University
astrophysicist at Goddard Space Flight Center and head of the mission
professor at Princeton and WMAP instrument scientist; he died in September 2002 and the spacecraft was renamed in his honour

fuentes.texto: NASA Goddard — WMAP completes its operations

turnos.pregunta: At first my name was MAP. Do you know why they changed it?
opciones: After a scientist who had died
turnos.texto_explorador: After David Wilkinson, a scientist at Princeton who worked on my instruments. He died in September 2002 and since then I carry his full name.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I was renamed WMAP in honour of David T. Wilkinson, instrument scientist at Princeton, who died in September 2002. I was the first spacecraft to use the Earth-Sun L2 Lagrange point, 1.5 million kilometres away, as an observation station.

turnos.pregunta: What can you learn by looking at the whole sky at once?
turnos.texto_explorador: The age of the universe. My job was the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light there is, and comparing its hot and cold spots gave the answer.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I measured temperature differences in the cosmic background between 2.7251 K and 2.7249 K, millionths of a degree, in five bands from 22 to 90 GHz. From that came an age of 13.770 million years with an uncertainty of 0.5%.

turnos.pregunta: What is the universe really made of?
opciones: Mostly of things we cannot see
Almost all of it is dust and gas
turnos.texto_explorador: Of things we do not see. Atoms, stars and planets are the small part: the rest is dark matter and dark energy, and they give off no light.
turnos.texto_cientifico: My final census of the universe: 4.6% atoms, 25.0% dark matter and close to 70% dark energy. I shrank the allowed volume of cosmological parameters by a factor of more than 68.000.

hitos.texto: To measure the cosmic microwave background and draw from it the parameters of the universe, its age and its composition. It was proposed in 1995, approved in 1996 and I was launched on June 30, 2001 under the name MAP.
I was the first spacecraft to use the Earth-Sun L2 point as an observation platform, 1.5 million kilometres from Earth and always with my back to the Sun and to Earth.
On August 20, 2010 I took the last science data and on September 8 I fired the thrusters to leave L2. I was left in a parking orbit around the Sun.
hitos.fuente: NASA Goddard — WMAP Project Completes Satellite Operations

puntos3d.texto: The two back-to-back dishes that watched the microwave background at five frequencies. The model is a single mesh and does not allow separating more parts.

aparatos.lugar: Disintegrated on re-entry into the atmosphere on January 5, 2025

estado_texto.texto_explorador: It fell back to Earth in January 2025, twenty years after leaving. Before that it went silent in 2015 and its agency stopped trying to recover it.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: JAXA X-ray observatory: a malfunction in June 2015 led to the end of the mission on August 26, 2015 and to its atmospheric re-entry, with total destruction, on January 5, 2025.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It observed the sky in X-rays for ten years, five times its planned life, and measured the spin of supermassive black holes. Japan ran it; NASA provided the telescopes.

personas.papel: head of the X-ray Astrophysics Laboratory at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
JAXA astrophysicist in Sagamihara who led the study of the Virgo cluster with Suzaku
astrophysicist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and principal investigator of the study of remnant 3C 397

turnos.pregunta: I was not a NASA mission. Do you know who was in charge?
opciones: Japan, with NASA as a partner
NASA, with Japan as a partner
turnos.texto_explorador: Japan: JAXA ran me, through its ISAS agency. NASA was a partner. It gave me my X-ray telescopes and the software, and it followed me from its guest centre at Goddard.
turnos.texto_cientifico: The mission was led by JAXA/ISAS. NASA contributed the X-ray telescopes and the data processing software, and operated the US guest facility (GOF) at Goddard Space Flight Center, which announced the end of the mission.

turnos.pregunta: What do you see with X-rays that you cannot see with ordinary light?
turnos.texto_explorador: Very hot gas. I looked at the Virgo cluster, 54 million light years away, and found iron, magnesium, silicon and sulphur spread out in a similar way everywhere, up to 5 million light years from the centre.
turnos.texto_cientifico: In the Virgo cluster I detected iron, magnesium, silicon and sulphur for the first time across the whole cluster, with observation arms out to 5 million light years: the chemical mix is homogeneous on the largest cosmic scales.

turnos.pregunta: How do you tell a supernova of a white dwarf from one that explodes on its own?
opciones: By the state of the iron
turnos.texto_explorador: By the iron: depending on how ionized it is, you can tell what kind of explosion it was. In remnant 3C 397 there was too much manganese and nickel, and that gave away a single white dwarf.
turnos.texto_cientifico: The ionization state of iron separates type Ia remnants from core-collapse ones. In 3C 397, at about 33.000 light years, the excess of manganese and nickel points to a white dwarf that piled up matter until it came close to 1.4 solar masses.

hitos.texto: To observe the universe in X-rays over a huge range, from 0.2 to 600 keV, with four CCD cameras and a high-energy detector. It was launched on July 10, 2005 as ASTRO-E2.
My XRS microcalorimeter spectrometer lost all its cryogen before routine observations began and the instrument was left unusable. I kept working with the CCD cameras.
I lasted ten years, five times my planned life, and JAXA declared the mission complete on August 26, 2015. On January 5, 2025 I disintegrated on re-entering the atmosphere.

puntos3d.texto: The four X-ray telescope modules with thin aluminium foils. The model is a single mesh.

aparatos.lugar: Destroyed on re-entry over the Pacific, 3.862 km south-east of Hawaii

estado_texto.texto_explorador: They steered me into the Pacific in June 2000, when one of my three gyroscopes failed. I broke up as I entered the air.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: The failure of the third gyroscope in December 1999 led to a controlled re-entry: four braking burns and destruction over the Pacific on June 4, 2000, with debris 3.862 km south-east of Hawaii.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It weighed 16 tonnes and was the largest astrophysics observatory launched up to 1999. It swept the sky in gamma rays, showed that the bursts come from other galaxies and ended up sunk in the Pacific.

personas.papel: Compton project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
led the BATSE experiment, developed at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center
led the EGRET instrument at Goddard Space Flight Center
led the OSSE instrument at the Naval Research Laboratory

HEASARC — the controlled re-entry of Compton

turnos.pregunta: They launched me inside a shuttle. Do you know how I got out into space?
opciones: In the cargo bay of Atlantis, with an extra spacewalk
turnos.texto_explorador: In the cargo bay of Atlantis, in April 1991. When they deployed my antenna it got stuck and two astronauts had to go out and free it: NASA's first unscheduled spacewalk in almost six years.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I flew on STS-37, the eighth flight of Atlantis, on April 5, 1991, and they deployed me on April 7. Jerry Ross and Jay Apt made an unscheduled spacewalk to free my stuck high-gain antenna.

turnos.pregunta: Gamma-ray bursts lasted seconds and nobody knew where they came from. What did I find out?
opciones: That they came from distant galaxies
That they came from the Sun
turnos.texto_explorador: That they came from very far away. My BATSE instrument saw them spread over the whole sky, without bunching up in the band of our galaxy. If they came from here they would be stuck to the Milky Way.
turnos.texto_cientifico: BATSE showed that the bursts are spread across the whole sky without following the structure of the Milky Way: they happen in distant galaxies. EGRET also discovered a new class of active galaxies, the blazars, and five gamma-ray pulsars.

turnos.pregunta: And what was a gamma-ray observatory doing looking down at the Earth?
opciones: Nothing, it always looked into the depths of the sky
turnos.texto_explorador: Looking at storms. I discovered by surprise that lightning also gives off gamma rays, so the Earth turned out to be one more source in that colour.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I unexpectedly detected gamma rays coming from terrestrial thunderstorms. My OSSE instrument also mapped the gamma rays of a cloud of antimatter that surrounds the central region of our galaxy.

hitos.texto: It carried BATSE, OSSE, COMPTEL and EGRET, which together covered from 20.000 eV to 30 GeV, with more than ten times the sensitivity of earlier missions.
I made the first all-sky survey in gamma rays and hundreds of new sources appeared: the gamma sky turned out to be far more dynamic and varied than expected.
hitos.fuente: NASA — 25 Years of Breakthrough Gamma-Ray Science

hitos.texto: One gyroscope began to fail in April 1999 and was lost in December, and that hastened the end of the mission: four braking burns and a controlled re-entry over the Pacific.

aparatos.lugar: Destroyed on re-entry over the South Pacific, east of New Zealand

estado_texto.texto_explorador: They brought it down on purpose in March 2001 and it came apart over the South Pacific. It was fifteen years old, three times the life it was designed for.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Controlled deorbit on March 23, 2001: the Progress M1-5 cargo ship fired three times; the station entered at about 62 miles altitude and began to break up around 50, over the South Pacific.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first modular space station and 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 13 countries passed through it. On board, Valeri Polyakov completed 437 days in a row, a record that still stands.

personas.papel: NASA astronaut who in 1995 began the agency's first long-duration stay on Mir
NASA astronaut; in 1996 she set the women's endurance record with 188 days, 4 hours and 0 minutes in orbit
manager of NASA's Shuttle-Mir programme

fuentes.texto: NASA History — the Mir station re-enters the atmosphere
NASA History — official history of the Shuttle-Mir programme

turnos.pregunta: I was not NASA's. Do you know whose I was?
opciones: The Soviet Union's, and later Russia's
turnos.texto_explorador: The Soviet Union's, and afterwards Russia's. NASA came as a partner: between 1995 and 1998 nine shuttles flew up to me and seven of its astronauts stayed here to live.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I was the Soviet and then the Russian programme. NASA took part through the Shuttle-Mir programme: nine docked shuttle missions and seven astronauts on long-duration stays between 1995 and 1998. Everything else belonged to the Russian programme.

turnos.pregunta: Here the record for the longest continuous time in space was set. How many days do you think it is?
turnos.texto_explorador: 437 days, 17 hours and 38 minutes. Valeri Polyakov signed them and nobody has beaten them yet. Before that, 326 days had already been completed here and later 366.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Valeri Polyakov spent 437 days, 17 hours and 38 minutes, a record that still stands according to NASA. The station had earlier accumulated marks of 326 and 366 days; in 1996 Shannon Lucid did 188 days, 4 hours and 0 minutes.

turnos.pregunta: How could I keep working after a fire and a collision?
opciones: Because it held up, and it served as a test
Because there was no serious accident
turnos.texto_explorador: Because I held up. I went through a dangerous fire and a near-catastrophic collision, and even so I stayed in service. That turned me into an endurance test bed for the station that came next.
turnos.texto_cientifico: A dangerous fire and a near-catastrophic collision did not take me out of service: I worked as a resilience test bed for the ISS, and 42 of my visitors later flew on it.

hitos.texto: I spent 15 years in orbit, three times my planned life: 86.331 orbits and 2.200 million miles travelled, at about 250 miles altitude and 17.885 mph.
hitos.fuente: NASA History — Space Station Mir Reenters Earth's Atmosphere

hitos.texto: 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 13 countries and space agencies passed through me. In space I grew the first seed-to-seed wheat harvest.

Progress M43 raised my orbit in October 2000 and M1-5 arrived in January 2001 with 5.900 pounds of propellant. Its three burns on March 23, 2001 brought me down into the South Pacific, in sight of Fiji.

aparatos.lugar: Spacecraft A re-entered over the eastern Pacific on March 11, 2026; B is still in orbit

estado_texto.texto_explorador: They were two spacecraft and they were switched off in 2019, after almost seven years listening to the radiation belts. A has already come down; B is still up there, switched off.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Spacecraft B was switched off on July 19, 2019 and spacecraft A on October 18, 2019, after almost seven years of data; A re-entered on March 11, 2026 over the eastern Pacific.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: Two twin spacecraft that discovered a third radiation belt around the Earth. They were meant for two years and lasted almost seven; the last one was switched off in 2019.

personas.papel: Van Allen Probes project manager at the Applied Physics Laboratory of Johns Hopkins University
mission scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
project scientist at the Applied Physics Laboratory, where the spacecraft were designed and built

NASA — Van Allen Probe A will re-enter the atmosphere

turnos.pregunta: A few days after arriving we already saw something that was not on the maps. What was it?
turnos.texto_explorador: A third radiation belt, stuck to the other two. It appears when the Sun gets restless and then comes apart; nobody had seen it form so clearly.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Days after launch we demonstrated the existence of a transient third radiation belt, which can form during periods of intense solar activity. It was our first result and it was not in any earlier model.

turnos.pregunta: How are the belt electrons accelerated to enormous energies?
turnos.texto_explorador: With plasma waves. Spacecraft B saw seven thousand electrical pulses per minute, and together they added up to a million volts in six minutes: enough to launch electrons at almost the speed of light.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Spacecraft B recorded 7.000 double-layer electrostatic pulses per minute that added up to a million volts in six minutes, enough to accelerate electrons to relativistic energies. Very low frequency chorus waves also lift them to millions of electronvolts within hours.

turnos.pregunta: And how did the mission end?
opciones: Switched off in 2019, and one has already come down
turnos.texto_explorador: Switched off. B went to sleep on July 19, 2019 and A on October 18. A came apart over the eastern Pacific on March 11, 2026; B is still circling, switched off.
turnos.texto_cientifico: They switched us off when the propellant ran out: B on July 19, 2019 and A on October 18, 2019, after almost seven years of data against the two of the design. Spacecraft A re-entered on March 11, 2026 at 6:37 EDT, at 2 degrees south and 255.3 degrees east; B should not come down before 2030.

hitos.texto: To watch over the Earth's radiation belts, the region where charged particles build up that can damage satellites and astronauts. They launched us together on August 30, 2012.
Days after arriving we had already seen a transient third radiation belt, which forms when solar activity is intense and then comes apart.
hitos.fuente: NASA — Ten Highlights, Van Allen Probes

hitos.texto: In February 2019 we made the final deorbit manoeuvres so as not to leave space junk in orbit. Spacecraft A re-entered on March 11, 2026, earlier than expected because of solar maximum.

The long boom that measured the electric field. With it came the discovery of a third radiation belt around Earth.
The spinning octagonal body, with the instruments that measured the electrons and ions of the belts.

aparatos.lugar: In an elliptical Earth orbit, switched off since November 28, 2022

estado_texto.texto_explorador: It stopped transmitting in November 2022, after more than thirty years of work. It is still in its orbit, switched off, with nobody having brought it down.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: End of operations on November 28, 2022, after its second data recorder failed on June 28, 2022; it operated for more than 30 years against the 4 planned and remains in an elliptical orbit of 9 x 30 Earth radii.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first joint mission of Japan and NASA and was designed for four years: it lasted more than thirty. It located the point where the Earth's magnetic field breaks and joins up again, at 80.000-120.000 miles.

personas.papel: US Geotail project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, since 2008
Japanese Geotail project manager at ISAS/JAXA
Japanese Geotail project scientist at ISAS/JAXA
first US Geotail project scientist at Goddard Space Flight Center

turnos.pregunta: Do you know whose I am? A single agency did not build me.
turnos.texto_explorador: Japan and the United States. I was the first mission they did together: Japan provided the spacecraft and the control from the ground, and the United States the instruments and the tracking. That is why they call me the mission of the two flags.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I was the first joint mission of Japan's ISAS and NASA, within the ISTP project. I weighed 1.009 kg, spun at 20 rpm, deployed antennas 100 metres tip to tip and carried seven instruments: MGF, LEP, EFD, EPIC, HEP, PWI and CPI.

turnos.pregunta: They say I found the exact spot where the Earth's magnetic field breaks. Where is it?
opciones: Behind the Earth, in the magnetic tail
turnos.texto_explorador: Behind the Earth, in the magnetic tail. There, between 80.000 and 120.000 miles, the field breaks and joins up again, and I saw it coincide with auroras over the poles. That result later guided the orbit of the MMS mission.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I located magnetic reconnection in the tail, between 80.000 and 120.000 miles from the Earth, and observed reconnections matching polar auroras confirmed at the same time by the Polar mission and by observers on the ground, with plasmoids ejected from those points.

turnos.pregunta: Besides the magnetic shield, what did I find that nobody had asked me to look for?
opciones: Oxygen and silicon on the Moon
A ring of dust around the Earth
turnos.texto_explorador: On my passes near the Moon I smelled its air: I found oxygen, silicon, sodium and aluminium in the lunar atmosphere. Nobody had sent me to look for it; it came as a gift, during the manoeuvres I made to change orbit.

turnos.texto_explorador: To measure in three dimensions. With four identical spacecraft separated by different distances you know where each boundary of the magnetic shield passes and how it changes in space, not just at one loose point.

turnos.texto_explorador: To see the aurora and measure it at the same time. Three of my twelve instruments were cameras; the other nine measured particles and fields right where I was. That way you could join up what was seen with what was happening.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I carried twelve instruments: three imaging the aurora at different wavelengths and nine measuring in situ. That combination made it possible for the first time to relate what was glowing up there with the fields and particles measured at the same moment.

turnos.pregunta: What lights the aurora? I found the path the energy comes along.

turnos.texto_cientifico: I identified surface Alfvén waves at 30.000-40.000 km altitude, travelling at 10.000 km/s; their energy is enough to feed all the known auroral acceleration mechanisms and most of what is released in substorms.

turnos.texto_explorador: A rain radar. It worked at 13.8 gigahertz, looked at a footprint of 5 kilometres and went down to 250 metres of detail: with that you see the inside of a storm, and not just its surface.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I was the first satellite with a precipitation radar in orbit: 13.8 GHz, 5 km footprint and 250 m vertical resolution, with a 250 km swath. My TMI radiometer swept 880 km, more than three times that width.

turnos.pregunta: They launched me from Japan. Whose am I, then?

turnos.texto_explorador: NASA's and the Japanese agency JAXA's, half and half. Japan provided the rocket and the radar; the United States the spacecraft and the other instruments. I was the first rain satellite built between the two agencies.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I was a joint mission of NASA and JAXA: Japan supplied the precipitation radar and the launch on an H-II rocket from Tanegashima on November 27, 1997, and the spacecraft was built almost entirely at Goddard Space Flight Center.

turnos.pregunta: Did you see any famous storm from inside?
turnos.texto_explorador: Hurricane Katrina, on August 28, 2005. I saw inside it: the hot towers that rise around the eye and let go of the heaviest rain. That way of looking at hurricanes changed for good.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On August 28, 2005 I obtained the three-dimensional rain structure of hurricane Katrina, including its hot towers next to the eye. I covered from 35 degrees north to 35 south, where more than two thirds of the world's rain falls, with rates that sometimes exceed 100 mm per hour.

hitos.texto: The first precipitation radar in orbit turned rain into volume images: for the first time the internal structure of storms was seen, layer by layer.

My altimeter fired a radar pulse and measured how long it took to come back; with that you know the height of the sea at any point on the planet and you see how it rises or falls over the years. turnos.texto_cientifico: My radar altimeter reached a precision of 4.2 cm and measured sea level with an accuracy better than 5 cm, repeating the same cycle every 10 days and delivering more than 98% of the science data planned for each cycle.

turnos.pregunta: Do you know what famous episode I portrayed from beginning to end?
turnos.texto_explorador: The great El Niño of 1997 and 1998, the biggest in a hundred years. For the first time it was seen whole from above and it was confirmed that its effects do not stay in the tropics: they reach much further than people thought.
turnos.texto_cientifico: I tracked and helped to forecast the biggest El Niño in a hundred years, that of 1997-1998: I gave the first global view of the phenomenon and showed that its effects are not limited to the tropics. turnos.pregunta: I had energy to spare. So why did I stop working?
turnos.texto_explorador: A reaction wheel seized and I could no longer point the panels and the antennas. With no way to manoeuvre there is no data: the last command reached me on January 18, 2006, after thirteen long years of work.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On October 9 my pitch wheel seized and I lost the ability to manoeuvre. On January 18, 2006, at 09:41:18 PST, I received the last command: 13 years, 5 months, 7 days, 17 hours and 33 minutes of mission.

hitos.texto: NASA began developing Topex in 1979 and the French CNES was planning Poseidon on its own. In 1983 they merged the two projects into one, launched on August 10, 1992.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: They switched me off on January 6, 1978. The precession of my orbit left me under the Sun for longer and longer, I overheated and there was no way left to keep looking. Since then I drift in silence, with no official source saying when I will come down.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Inoperative satellite since January 6, 1978, switched off because the accumulated precession of its orbital plane left it exposed to the Sun almost constantly and caused overheating. The date of its atmospheric reentry does not appear in the sources consulted.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It lifted off as ERTS-1 and was the first satellite conceived to watch over the planet's landmasses, with an RBV and a multispectral MSS scanner on board. It outlived its one-year design and kept observing until January 1978, when overheating forced it into silence.

puntos3d.texto: My body came from the design of the Nimbus weather satellites, a structure already proven in orbit. On that base they mounted everything that later changed the way we look at Earth.
Two solar wings gave me the power my instruments needed. I was designed for one year, and I lasted five and a half years.
The MSS delivered my first image on July 25, 1972: the Dallas-Fort Worth area, in false colour. With it I reached more than 300.000 scenes.
I also carried three tube cameras, the RBVs, with which Earth could be photographed. They were used less than the scanner.

hitos.texto: On July 25, 1972 my MSS scanner delivered the first image in the Landsat archive: the Dallas-Fort Worth area, in Texas, in false colour. Before 1973 was out it had covered almost the whole of the Earth's surface, much of it with few clouds.

The accumulated precession of my orbital plane meant I saw sunlight almost constantly and the temperature became unbearable. On January 6, 1978 they switched me off, five and a half years after my launch and a long way from the one year of life they had planned for me.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the second of the series and the twin that allowed two Earth-observation satellites to look at the same time, with the RBV and MSS inherited from Landsat 1. It lasted seven years against the single year of design planned and kept the record going when its predecessor went dark.

puntos3d.texto: My body and my instruments were the same as my brother's. That sameness was the plan: our photos had to be comparable without doubting the machine.
Two solar wings and a planned life of one year, like Landsat 1. In the end I lasted seven.
My scanner repeated the same measurement as Landsat 1's, in the same band and with the same filters, so that the record would not break when it failed.
My cameras and my scanner fed the first great crop inventory, centred on wheat, which proved that a harvest could be forecast a year in advance.

My data fed the Large Area Crop Inventory Experiment (LACIE), the first big interagency crop-monitoring campaign, centred on wheat. With them it was shown that agricultural yields could be forecast a year in advance.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the first Landsat of a new generation, with the Thematic Mapper, a seven-band instrument that multiplied the detail of the view of the ground. With it came the programme's first natural-colour images and the first GPS receiver to fly on a civil satellite.

hitos.texto: I was the first civil satellite to carry a GPS receiver on board, when only four of the twenty-four planned satellites were operational. The Goddard researchers showed that it could work out my position to within 50 m and my speed to within six centimetres per second.

turnos.pregunta: What did I bring that no earlier Landsat had?
turnos.texto_explorador: The Thematic Mapper: seven bands and the programme's first natural-colour image, with 30 metres of detail.
turnos.texto_cientifico: The seven-band TM, with 30 m in the reflective bands and 120 m in the thermal one, gave the first natural-colour image and opened up applications such as bathymetry.

turnos.texto_explorador: A GPS receiver, when there were only four satellites of the constellation up there.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: They switched me off on June 5, 2013, after almost twenty-nine years. I was built for three. Now I go round in silence, and my almost four million pictures are still telling how the Earth changed without me.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was an Earth-observation satellite launched on March 1, 1984 with the MSS and TM instruments, designed for three years and operational for almost twenty-nine. aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was NASA and CNES's ocean altimetry satellite that continued the TOPEX/Poseidon series by measuring sea level, wind speed and wave height across more than 95 % of the ice-free ocean every ten days. Designed for three to five years, it operated for eleven and a half and was deactivated in July 2013.

puntos3d.texto: My body was a compact box from NASA and CNES, with the altimetry instruments on the face that looked at the sea.
Poseidon-2 emitted on two frequencies to measure sea level without water vapour falsifying the measurement.
My two solar wings deployed already in orbit. With their power I flew again over the same ground track as TOPEX/Poseidon, one minute ahead.
I flew like that for almost a year and a half, paired with my predecessor, to compare the two measurements under the same conditions and splice twenty years of record without gaps.
Below I carried the laser retroreflector and the DORIS antennas, with which the ground stations tracked me and corrected my orbit.

hitos.texto: In January 2002 I reached my operational orbit of 1.337 km and flew over the same track as TOPEX/Poseidon barely one minute apart, which made it possible to compare both measurements in almost identical conditions and to splice together a climate record of more than twenty years without jumps.

hitos.titulo: Final geodetic mission and loss of contact
hitos.texto: In the spring of 2012 I was moved to my graveyard orbit and repurposed to study the marine gravity field; the first complete 406-day geodetic cycle ended on June 17, 2013 and four days later contact was lost for good.

turnos.pregunta: What did I measure every ten days?
turnos.texto_explorador: Sea level, wave height and surface wind, over more than 95 % of the ice-free ocean.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Ocean altimetry: sea level, wind and waves over more than 95 % of the ice-free ocean every 10 days.

turnos.pregunta: Why did I stop talking?
turnos.texto_explorador: My last transmitter failed; the backup had already gone in 2005. They passivated me on July 1, 2013.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Loss of contact on June 21, 2013 due to failure of the last transmitter; passivated on July 1 in a graveyard orbit, with no reentry expected for at least 1.000 years.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: In 2009 my antenna stopped and in 2018 they shut me down for good. I spent almost twenty years measuring winds nobody could see, and when the world wrote me off I went on serving as a ruler for those who came after.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: On November 23, 2009 its spinning antenna stopped at 0 rpm and it could no longer resolve wind vectors; the instrument stayed switched on and was used as a calibration standard until it was turned off on October 2, 2018 under its end-of-mission plan. The satellite remains inoperative in orbit.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was a fast-recovery mission launched on June 19, 1999 to make up for the loss of NSCAT, with the SeaWinds scatterometer on board. Designed for two or three years, it measured surface wind over more than 90 % of the ice-free ocean every day for a decade and then served nine more years as a calibration reference.

puntos3d.texto: My scatterometer antenna rotated without stopping and swept a strip 1.800 kilometres wide, with some 400.000 wind measurements a day.
My body was a quick-recovery box: it was built in a short time to fill the gap NSCAT had left.
The panels gave me power. I did not need to point: my antenna measured skimming the sea, by day and by night and through the clouds.
With the antenna turning I used up almost all my power. Even so I operated for ten years, against the two or three that were expected of me.
In November 2009 the antenna's lubricant dried up and I could no longer measure the wind. I stayed switched on for nine more years, serving as a calibration yardstick for other scatterometers.

hitos.titulo: A decade measuring the ocean's wind
hitos.texto: From July 19, 1999 the SeaWinds scatterometer, at 13.4 GHz, swept a 1.800 km swath every day and covered more than 90 % of the Earth's surface, with some 400.000 daily measurements that improved forecasts and made it possible to detect hurricanes on the open sea.

When the lubricant in the bearings dried up at the end of 2009 the antenna pointed downwards and its swath shrank to about 30 km, but the stability of that measurement turned it into the reference standard against which ESA and ISRO calibrated their scatterometers; the instrument was switched off on October 2, 2018.

turnos.pregunta: What stopped on me in 2009?
turnos.texto_explorador: The antenna. The lubricant in the bearings dried up and I could no longer measure wind direction.
turnos.texto_cientifico: On November 23, 2009 the SeaWinds antenna stopped at 0 rpm and the ability to resolve wind vectors was lost.

turnos.pregunta: What was I good for after I stopped measuring?
turnos.texto_explorador: As a ruler: other scatterometers were calibrated against my measurement.
turnos.texto_cientifico: With the antenna fixed it served as a calibration reference for ESA and ISRO scatterometers until it was switched off on October 2, 2018.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: In December 2010 I stopped answering and nobody heard anything at the other end any more. Thirteen years looking at what colour the sea was, and now I am still up there, switched off, while the ocean changes and I cannot tell anyone about it.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: In December 2010 the satellite, by then renamed OrbView-2, lost communications with the ground stations and the mission was formally concluded in February 2011. It operated for more than thirteen years against a five-year design life, leaving behind one of the most complete continuous records of ocean biology available.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was the ocean colour sensor on board the SeaStar satellite, later OrbView-2, launched on August 1, 1997 in an air launch. It measured chlorophyll concentration and marine production for more than thirteen years, until contact with the satellite was lost in December 2010.

puntos3d.texto: My body was small, the size of a cupboard. Almost everything I carried inside was the SeaWiFS sensor.
SeaWiFS looked at the sea in eight bands, between 402 and 885 nanometres, and from that colour the chlorophyll of the water is calculated.
Four panels in a cross gave me power. They were enough for thirteen years, against the five that were expected.
With that continuous gaze it was seen for the first time how the life of the ocean changes with the seasons and with El Niño.

hitos.texto: After 32 burns that raised the orbit from the 278 km parking orbit to 705 km, the instrument went into routine operation on September 18, 1997 and began distributing global ocean colour data at 4 km.

hitos.titulo: Thirteen years of biological record of the ocean
hitos.texto: Designed for a minimum of five years, SeaWiFS operated for more than thirteen: it mapped the ocean's greenery, followed the seasonality of blooms and the response of plankton to El Niño and La Niña, and served as technical preparation for MODIS and VIIRS.

turnos.pregunta: What was I looking at in the sea?
turnos.texto_explorador: Colour: that is how chlorophyll is worked out and how you see where there is plant life in the ocean.
turnos.texto_cientifico: SeaWiFS measured ocean colour in 8 bands between 402 and 885 nm to derive chlorophyll and primary production.

turnos.texto_explorador: They released me from an aircraft, with a Pegasus rocket that ignited in the air.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I have been switched off since February 25, 2020, when NASA passivated me as planned: I no longer measure anything, I am just still up there, in a 645 km orbit.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Satellite passivated on February 25, 2020 after more than 17 years of total solar irradiance (TSI) and spectral solar irradiance (SSI) observations between 1 and 2400 nm; the shutdown was a planned event after the required overlap with TSIS-1.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was a NASA satellite funded and operated by LASP that measured the solar radiation reaching the Earth in X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, near infrared and total radiation, with four instruments. It worked for more than seventeen years, covering two solar cycles, and was passivated in February 2020.

puntos3d.texto: My body was a compact box with four instruments, and all of them looked at the same place: the Sun.
I measured the energy of the Sun in X-rays, ultraviolet, visible and infrared, and also the total radiation that reaches Earth.
Six panels in a cross gave me power. I did not need to point with precision: I looked at the Sun without moving.
I spent seventeen years measuring, more than a complete solar cycle, until they switched me off in February 2020.

hitos.texto: The mission ended on February 25, 2020 with more than seventeen years of total and spectral irradiance measurements, after the overlap with TSIS-1 on the International Space Station.

turnos.texto_explorador: The Sun's radiation: from X-rays and ultraviolet to the infrared and the total energy arriving.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Total solar irradiance with TIM and spectral irradiance with SIM, SOLSTICE and XPS, between 1 and 2400 nm.

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I stopped observing on July 21, 2004 and since then I have been sleeping in hibernation; I only woke in the summer of 2005 to watch a probe crash into a comet.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: Its regular science observations stopped on July 21, 2004; in June 2005 it was reactivated for about three months to follow the Deep Impact impact on comet 9P/Tempel 1. No official date of final deactivation or of reentry appears in the sources consulted.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was a submillimetre telescope from NASA's Small Explorer programme that measured water, molecular oxygen, atomic carbon and carbon monoxide in interstellar clouds to understand how stars and planets are born. It observed more than a hundred molecular clouds in the Milky Way and in 2005 was reactivated to support Deep Impact.

puntos3d.texto: My submillimetre telescope measured 55 by 71 centimetres and searched for water and molecular oxygen in the clouds where stars are born.
Inside my body went cooled receivers to hear very faint signals, those of the cold gas of the Milky Way.
Four solar panels on two arms gave me power. With them I mapped more than a hundred molecular clouds.
In June 2005 they woke me to measure the water of comet Tempel 1 before, during and after the impact of Deep Impact.

hitos.texto: With its 55 x 71 cm off-axis Cassegrain telescope it mapped, in five spectral lines — water, molecular oxygen, atomic carbon, 13CO and H2-18O — dozens of giant molecular clouds and dark cores, with maps one degree by one degree.
In June 2005, after a year in standby mode, it operated again for about three months to measure the water production of comet 9P/Tempel 1 before, during and after the Deep Impact impact.

turnos.pregunta: What was I looking for in the clouds of gas?
turnos.texto_explorador: Water and molecular oxygen, among other molecules: what you need to understand how stars and planets are born.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Five lines: water, O2, C I, 13CO and H2-18O, in more than a hundred molecular clouds.

turnos.pregunta: Why did I wake up in 2005?
turnos.texto_explorador: To watch Deep Impact crash into comet Tempel 1.
turnos.texto_cientifico: Reactivated in June 2005 for about three months to measure the water production of 9P/Tempel 1 before, during and after the impact.

aparatos.lugar: Reentered the atmosphere on May 10, 2011

estado_texto.texto_explorador: I burned up in the Earth's atmosphere on May 10, 2011: I no longer exist. Before that I spent years looking at stars it was not my job to look at.
estado_texto.texto_cientifico: It lost its solid hydrogen cryogen hours after launch when the telescope cover came off prematurely while the spacecraft was spinning, so it obtained no data for its infrared programme. It was reused for asteroseismology of bright stars and reentered the Earth's atmosphere on May 10, 2011.

aparatos.ficha_resumen: It was an infrared telescope cooled with solid hydrogen, designed to study galaxies with bursts of star formation and to search for protogalaxies. The telescope cover came off prematurely after launch, the coolant ran out and there was no infrared science; the spacecraft was repurposed for asteroseismology until its reentry in 2011.

puntos3d.texto: My telescope had a 30-centimetre aperture and a field of 32 by 32 arcminutes, designed to count galaxies with bursts of star formation.
Behind the telescope I carried a tank of solid hydrogen, which was what was supposed to keep it frozen.
Four solar panels gave me energy. I needed it above all to keep the coolant.
The cover of the telescope came off too early: I lost the solid hydrogen within hours, and with it my whole infrared programme.

hitos.titulo: Loss of the coolant after launch
hitos.texto: The telescope cover came off ahead of time while the spacecraft was still spinning after orbital insertion; sunlight heated the solid hydrogen, outgassing occurred and the spacecraft spun faster than the reaction wheels could brake, with total loss of the coolant.

Once control was recovered, it was used for asteroseismology, measuring oscillations of nearby stars; operations passed to the centre at Bowie State University and the telescope reentered the atmosphere on May 10, 2011.

turnos.pregunta: What happened to me a few hours after lifting off?
turnos.texto_explorador: The telescope cover came off, sunlight heated the solid hydrogen and I lost all my coolant.
turnos.texto_cientifico: The cover came off during insertion; outgassing sped up the spin, the cryogen was lost and there was no infrared science.
